questions.prompt: DESIGN IT — [senior] garbage collection and a blob-store migration for a deduplicating upload pipeline (dotnet-drop, docs/upskill/03-architecture-and-patterns/04-side-effects-async-and-reliability.md). Scenario: the service holds 9 TB of blobs on local disk; about 120,000 upload sessions start each month and 14% of them are abandoned partway; content is stored once per SHA-256 and shared by every file version with the same bytes; and the business wants every blob moved to object storage over 3 weeks while uploads keep running. Write your design before you look: what reference structure the code actually keeps between file versions and stored bytes, how orphans are found (chunks of dead sessions, stored objects that no version points at), the rule that makes deleting a shared blob safe, and the copy and cutover plan for the move. Then tick the checkpoints you covered and add up the weights (suggested pass: 70% with every [w3] hit)

keyPoints.text: [w3] Start from the references that really exist: a blobs row per distinct content hash (unique index) carrying a storage key and a counter, and a BlobId on every file version. The database declares a single foreign key, file_versions to file_nodes; nothing ties a version's BlobId to a blobs row, so liveness has to be computed by your collector, not enforced by the schema.

[w3] Treat the counter as a hint at best: the entity has a method to decrement it, but no code path calls it, so the number only ever climbs and a blob whose last version is gone still shows a positive count. The deletion test is whether any file_versions row names the blob's id, answered by a query at collection time.

[w3] Chunk orphans come in two kinds, and the one nobody collects is not the abandoned upload: a Completed session's chunk files are removed only by the statement that follows the commit, so a crash between the two leaves them on disk with nothing scheduled to look at that session again. Enumerate chunk storage by session id and remove anything whose session is no longer Open.

[w3] Bytes can exist with no row at all: Complete hands new content to blob storage before the database save, so any failure of that save (for instance two first uploads of the same content where the unique hash index rejects one) strands an object. A storage-listing sweep may delete an unclaimed object only when it is older than a grace period longer than any Complete can take.

[w2] Not every stored object is a content blob: thumbnails are written into the same blob store under a name built from the node id, with no blobs row; the only pointer to them is the node's ThumbnailPath. A sweep that deletes whatever lacks a blobs row would wipe every thumbnail, so the mark phase must also collect those paths.

[w3] A shared blob is safe to remove only in two steps: first condemn it in a transaction that re-checks no version references it (and that Complete honours by treating a condemned row as absent), then delete the bytes after a grace period. Complete can find the row by hash at any instant and only bumps it without writing any bytes, so a one-step check-then-delete can be overtaken.

[w3] Each blobs row stores its own key, which makes a per-row move possible: copy the object, re-hash the copy against the row's content hash, then repoint that row. But the host wires exactly one blob store, chosen by a configuration switch, so three weeks of coexistence needs a new composite store (new writes to object storage, reads that know both), a resumable backfill, and the old disk kept until a final reconcile.

[w1] The abandoned kind is already handled: the janitor wakes every 15 minutes, selects sessions still Open whose deadline has passed, expires them and deletes their chunk files. A Completed session never matches that filter, which is why the post-commit gap needs a collector of its own.

questions.prompt: PRE-MORTEM — week two of the migration, with the first collector live. The collector removes a blob in the same second that a Complete for identical bytes finds it by hash; the copier is halfway through its list when a user uploads a file whose hash neither store holds yet; a session reaches its deadline and is swept while its client is re-sending chunk 511 of 640; and two teammates finish uploading a file the store already holds at the same moment. For each, what does the code at this commit do, what is lost or left behind, and what would have prevented it?

keyPoints.text: [w3] The collector-versus-Complete race: Complete sees the existing row, writes no bytes and records a version pointing at it; if the collector's delete of those bytes lands after its own reference check, the new version points at nothing, and the scan and every download fail when they open the storage key. Condemn-then-delete with a grace period, plus Complete refusing condemned rows, closes it.

[w3] Lost increments: the blobs mapping configures no concurrency token (the users and file_nodes mappings do), so two Completes that both read a count of n both save n+1 and one reference disappears from the number. Any collector that trusted the count could then free bytes a live version still uses, which is why the sweep must recompute references itself.

[w3] A copier working from a snapshot of rows misses everything created after the snapshot: a brand-new hash is written by whichever single store is configured, so while local disk is still the write target the new object lands there and is invisible to the copy. Switch writes to the new store first, then run a delta pass over rows created since the snapshot before the old disk is retired.

[w2] Make the copy idempotent by naming objects by content: the store is handed the hash and returns the key the row keeps, so a new store whose key is a function of the hash rewrites identical bytes when a copy is repeated, and a copier crash resumes from its checkpoint without creating duplicates. Repoint a row only after the copy verifies, with an update conditioned on the old key.

[w3] The sweep-mid-retry case: the chunk handler checks that the session is Open only at the top, so a request already past that check can store chunk 511 and insert its row after the sweep has removed the session's files, leaving a fresh chunk under an Expired session that no later sweep revisits. Expire on inactivity rather than a fixed age, and let a storage-side pass catch late writers.

[w2] Nothing deletes upload_chunks rows: neither the sweep nor Complete removes them, so the table keeps a row for every chunk ever accepted and those rows go on claiming chunks whose files are gone. A collector must delete the rows with the session's files, or orphan detection that reads rows will report stale truth.

questions.prompt: TRADE-OFF HANDBACK — defend your collection and migration choices against the alternatives: counting references versus periodically marking what is reachable and sweeping the rest, deleting bytes at once versus holding them through a retention window, copying everything and then cutting over versus writing to both stores during the move, and repointing each row after a verified copy versus a read path that falls back from the new store to the old. For each, say what you bought and what it cost.

keyPoints.text: [w3] A reference count answers 'can this go?' instantly, but only if every path that adds or drops a reference updates it in the same transaction and under concurrency control. Here both Complete and the file copy increment it, nothing decrements it, and the row is unguarded, so the count is neither maintained nor protected.

[w3] Mark-and-sweep recomputes reachability from the versions and thumbnail paths each run, so it tolerates missed bookkeeping and needs no hot-path writes; it costs a scan over every version and blob per run and a grace period for work in flight. A sound mix keeps the counter as a cheap candidate filter and lets the sweep decide.

[w3] Deleting at once returns space soonest, but a collector bug or an unclosed race then destroys data for good; a retention window (condemned objects kept N days, or object-store versioning and lifecycle rules) makes mistakes reversible for the price of storage. The code already chooses soft deletion with a restore path for file rows, and bytes deserve no less.

[w3] Copy-then-cutover keeps one write path and is simple to reason about, but needs a delta pass or a brief write freeze to catch objects created during the copy. Writing to both stores from day one shrinks that gap to the backfill, but every write can half-succeed and must be reconciled, on top of a completion step that already spans several systems with no transaction across them.
keyPoints.quote: Upload completion touches database, disk/S3 blob storage, chunk cleanup, and processing queue

keyPoints.text: [w2] Repointing a row after a verified copy means every read goes to exactly one store and the row says which; a fall-back read path (new store, then old) lets the copy run without touching rows but costs a miss on each unmoved object and hides objects the copier never reached. Downloads, share links and the scanner all open bytes through the row's key, so the row is the natural switch.

[w1] The chapter names completion as the place where consistency is decided; adding a second store and a collector widens that boundary, which is why both need their own reconcile step rather than trusting the request path.
keyPoints.quote: That is the main consistency boundary.
